---
title: "Sensitivity analysis"
params: 
    TOGGLE: TRUE
---

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
source('../assets/setup.R')
library(tidyverse)
library(sjPlot)
```


A sensitivity analysis lets us check how **sensitive** our conclusions are to changes in our modelling approach (here, the removal of observations).

In DAPR2, we'll do sensitivity analyses by excluding a potentially influential observation, re-fitting our model, and seeing whether the directions (the signs, positive vs. negative) of the coefficients and/or the pattern of statistical significance (and therefore our conclusions based on our model) will change.

In the [Influential observations](influence.html){target="_blank"} flash card, we saw an example of one very influential value.
Here we'll see how to handle it.

## Example

In the mental wellbeing data from the Block 1 labs, one data point—number 109—has a much higher Cook's Distance than the rest.

```{r}
mwdata <- read_csv('https://uoepsy.github.io/data/wellbeing_rural.csv')
wb_mdl <- lm(wellbeing ~ outdoor_time + social_int, data = mwdata)
plot(wb_mdl, which = 4)
```


To do the sensitivity analysis, we must remove observation 109 from the dataset and fit the same model again on that new, smaller dataset.

```{r} 
# remove the content of row 109
mwdata_no109 <- mwdata[-109,]

# fit a model with the same formula on the new, reduced dataset
wb_mdl_no109 <- lm(wellbeing ~ outdoor_time + social_int, data = mwdata_no109)
```

Now, compare the pattern of statistical significance in the two models:


::::{.columns}
:::{.column width="50%"}

Original model, including observation 109:

```{r}
summary(wb_mdl)
```

:::
:::{.column width="50%"}

Reduced model, not including observation 109:

```{r}
summary(wb_mdl_no109)
```

:::
::::

The coefficients all have the same signs: they were positive in the original model, they are still positive in the reduced model.

And the pattern of significance also does not change.
All estimates with original p-values below $\alpha$ = .05 are still beyond that threshold in the reduced model.

Therefore, even though observation 109 has a large Cook's Distance, our model is not sensitive to its removal and it doesn't actually impact our conclusions.
This means that our conclusions based on the original model still hold.


## What if I see lots of very influential values?

My advice: do a sensitivity analysis that drops only the observation with the *greatest* Cook's Distance.
If it makes no impact on your conclusions, then probably the other values which have lower Cook's Distance scores will also have no impact on your conclusions.

If it *does* impact your conclusions, then you must report this as part of your description of your analysis.
You should also move on to drop each additional high-influence  case point, removing one row from your dataset each time, until your conclusions stop changing.
Every step of this process must be described in a report.
